claim: Two monkeys (subjects M and N) performed a value-based decision-making task in which visual stimuli were associated with juice rewards.
source: Two monkeys (subjects M and N) performed a value-based decision-making task in which visual stimuli were associated with juice rewards (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental subjects and task design.

claim: Images predicted an amount and type of reward, which was either primary in the form of juice at the end of the trial, or secondary as a bar that increased proportionally to the value associated with the stimulus.
source: Images predicted an amount and type of reward, which was either primary in the form of juice at the end of the trial, or secondary as a bar that increased proportionally to the value associated with the stimulus (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by the task structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A total of eight pictures comprised the set of stimuli associated with reward, with four different values matched between primary (juice) and secondary (bar) rewards in terms of the monkeys' preferences.
source: A total of eight pictures comprised the set of stimuli associated with reward, with four different values matched between primary (juice) and secondary (bar) rewards in terms of the monkeys' preferences (Rich and Wallis, 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design, supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Both monkeys learned to perform the task optimally by selecting the stimulus associated with higher values in more than 90% of the trials.
source: Both monkeys learned to perform the task optimally by selecting the stimulus associated with higher values in more than 90% of the trials (Rich and Wallis, 2016).
evidence: This is a behavioral performance measure supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A logistic regression model predicting the cues chosen by the animals with variables value and type showed a much lower coefficient for type, and its p-values were many orders of magnitude larger, confirming that the type of reward had little influence on the choice of animals compared to value.
source: A logistic regression model predicting the cues chosen by the animals with variables value and type showed a much lower coefficient for type, and its p-values were many orders of magnitude larger, confirming that the type of reward had little influence on the choice of animals compared to value (Figure 1C, coefficients with [p-value of t-test] for monkeys M and N respectively; type left/right: .41 [2.53e-3]/-.51 [1.75e-4] and −0.61 [2.6e-3]/0.32 [0.11], value left/right: 1.77 [6.1e-117]/−1.95 [3.02e-136] and 2.66 [1.59e-94]/−2.46 [2.27e-90]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis results with specific coefficients and p-values provided.

claim: Reaction times in the unrelated joystick task decreased as the value of the stimulus increased, providing evidence that monkeys maintained an expectation of the upcoming reward across the intervening time interval.
source: Here, reaction times in the unrelated joystick task decreased as the value of the stimulus increased, providing evidence that monkeys maintained an expectation of the upcoming reward across the intervening time interval (Rich and Wallis, 2016, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding supported by data and citation.

claim: Reaction times were unaffected by the type of reward anticipated.
source: Reaction times were also unaffected by the type of reward anticipated (linear regression predicting reaction time as a function of value and type in single cue trials : coefficients for value [p-value of t-test] for monkeys M and N, respectively; type: −21 [.08] and 14.5 [.32], value: −63.9 [1.73e-31] and −65.7 [2.66e-23]).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis with specific coefficients and p-values.

claim: Single and multi units were recorded in the orbitofrontal (OFC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) of the two subjects while they performed the decision-making task across 24 and 20 sessions (monkey M and N, respectively).
source: Single and multi units were recorded in the orbitofrontal (OFC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) of the two subjects while they performed the decision-making task across 24 and 20 sessions (monkey M and N, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the neurophysiological recording methods.

claim: Units from all recording sessions and both monkeys were pooled together to create 2 populations of 798 and 315 neurons recorded from the OFC and ACC, respectively.
source: Units from all recording sessions and both monkeys were pooled together to create 2 populations of 798 and 315 neurons recorded from the OFC and ACC, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data pooling procedure, supported by Table 1.

claim: Basic unit and decoding results did not differ across monkeys (except for encoding and decoding of reward type in ACC) so data were pooled.
source: Basic unit and decoding results did not differ across monkeys (except for encoding and decoding of reward type in ACC, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E) so data were pooled.
evidence: This is a statement about data analysis decisions based on observed similarities, supported by supplementary figures.

claim: The vast majority of OFC and ACC units encoded value at some point after the reward predicting cue and before the reward (73.2% for OFC and 77.8% for ACC).
source: Similar to previous reports (Rich and Wallis, 2017), the vast majority of OFC and ACC units encoded value at some point after the reward predicting cue and before the reward (73.2% for OFC and 77.8% for ACC, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about neural encoding, supported by data and citation.

claim: The proportion of neurons encoding value peaked after the presentation of the reward predicting cue and steadily decreased until the reward.
source: The proportion of neurons encoding value peaked after the presentation of the reward predicting cue and steadily decreased until the reward (C, Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes a temporal pattern in neural encoding shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The type of reward was only weakly encoded compared to value, with less than half the proportion of units encoding it at any time (29.8% for OFC and 37.1% for ACC).
source: The type of reward was only weakly encoded compared to value, with less than half the proportion of units encoding it at any time (29.8% for OFC and 37.1% for ACC, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of encoding between value and type, supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: No difference between ACC and OFC was found in the proportion of units encoding value at any point during the epoch of interest.
source: No difference between ACC and OFC was found in the proportion of units encoding value at any point during the epoch of interest, but encoding of type was higher in ACC mostly driven by the data of one monkey (Figure 2B, χ2 test of independence, value: p=0.13 and type: p=0.022).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between brain regions with specific test results provided.

claim: Encoding of type was higher in ACC mostly driven by the data of one monkey.
source: No difference between ACC and OFC was found in the proportion of units encoding value at any point during the epoch of interest, but encoding of type was higher in ACC mostly driven by the data of one monkey (Figure 2B, χ2 test of independence, value: p=0.13 and type: p=0.022).
evidence: This is a statistical finding with specific test results provided.

claim: The relative onset of value encoding was earlier in the OFC compared to ACC.
source: In accordance with previous findings (Kennerley and Wallis, 2009), the relative onset of value encoding was earlier in the OFC compared to ACC (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a temporal comparison between brain regions, supported by data and citation.

claim: Latencies in the OFC were significantly shorter for both value and type.
source: Latencies in the OFC were significantly shorter for both value and type (Kruskal-Wallis on latencies value:[stat = 19.4, p=1.05*10−5] and type:[stat = 7.93, p=4.85*10−3]).
evidence: This is a statistical finding with specific test results provided.

claim: The latency result was replicated in each monkey's data independently.
source: This result was replicated in each monkey's data independently (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This confirms the robustness of the finding across subjects.

claim: Population decoding of value with a linear ridge classifier elicited a peak in accuracy similar to the peak in the proportion of encoding units after the presentation of the delay, followed by a stable significant decoding until reward.
source: Population decoding of value with a linear ridge classifier elicited a peak in accuracy similar to the peak in the proportion of encoding units after the presentation of the delay, followed by a stable significant decoding until reward (Figure 2C, significance threshold set to p<0.01 with 1000 permutations, replicated in each monkey, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes a decoding analysis result with statistical threshold and replication noted.

claim: The first significant bin decoding value and type was 100 ms and 150 ms earlier respectively in OFC compared to ACC.
source: The first significant bin decoding value and type was 100 ms and 150 ms earlier respectively in OFC compared to ACC, and peak decoding was earlier and higher in OFC compared to ACC (for value/type: 93.5%/91.5% in OFC at 250 ms/350 ms, 77.6%/75.6% in ACC at 450 ms/450 ms).
evidence: This is a quantitative temporal comparison of decoding between brain regions.

claim: Peak decoding was earlier and higher in OFC compared to ACC (for value/type: 93.5%/91.5% in OFC at 250 ms/350 ms, 77.6%/75.6% in ACC at 450 ms/450 ms).
source: The first significant bin decoding value and type was 100 ms and 150 ms earlier respectively in OFC compared to ACC, and peak decoding was earlier and higher in OFC compared to ACC (for value/type: 93.5%/91.5% in OFC at 250 ms/350 ms, 77.6%/75.6% in ACC at 450 ms/450 ms).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of decoding accuracy between brain regions.

claim: The sensitivity index (d') averaged across pairs of values in all neurons was higher in OFC (0.26) than in ACC (0.22).
source: The sensitivity index (also known as d') averaged across pairs of values in all neurons was higher in OFC (0.26) than in ACC (0.22), suggesting that values might be easier to separate in OFC activity compared to ACC, leading to higher decoding accuracy.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with an interpretation about discriminability.

claim: Value is strongly encoded in OFC and ACC and can be significantly decoded throughout the delay.
source: Together, these results show that value is strongly encoded in these prefrontal regions and can be significantly decoded throughout the delay.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the preceding analyses.

claim: The total number of neurons encoding value during the delay was much higher than the number encoding at any particular point in time, indicating that value was represented by different neurons throughout the delay.
source: The total number of neurons encoding value during the delay was much higher than the number encoding at any particular point in time, indicating that value was represented by different neurons throughout the delay.
evidence: This is an observation about the temporal distribution of encoding neurons with an interpretation.

claim: Both OFC and ACC value coding tiled the delay, such that different subsets of neurons were most selective at different times.
source: We sorted the units based on the time of peak value encoding during the delay with the training half, and found that both OFC and ACC value coding tiled the delay, such that different subsets of neurons were most selective at different times (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The tiling of the delay is also present in the testing data, although somewhat less clear.
source: We then sorted the testing data according to the peak-encoding bin of the training data to assess its consistency (Figure 3B), and found that the tiling of the delay is also present in the testing data, although somewhat less clear.
evidence: This describes a validation of the tiling pattern using independent data.

claim: Peak encoding times did not follow a straight line, such that the proportion of encoding neurons decreased during the delay.
source: In the period restricted to the delay itself, peak encoding times did not follow a straight line, such that the proportion of encoding neurons decreased during the delay (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes a temporal pattern in the encoding data.

claim: Encoding epochs are not uniformly distributed in time, consistent with a recent model of sequential encoding.
source: This suggests that encoding epochs are not uniformily distributed in time, consistent with a recent model of sequential encoding (Rajan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data pattern with reference to a theoretical model.

claim: The peak encoding bins of training and testing data sets were significantly correlated, which is expected with sequential encoding.
source: The peak encoding bins of training and testing data sets were also significantly correlated, which is expected with sequential encoding.
evidence: This is a statistical finding with an interpretation related to sequential encoding.

claim: Only 6.9% and 10.2% of units encoded value for more than half the delay in OFC and ACC, respectively.
source: Only 6.9% and 10.2% of units encoded value for more than half the delay in OFC and ACC, respectively, while less than 1% of neurons encoded type for that same duration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about encoding duration.

claim: Less than 1% of neurons encoded type for more than half the delay.
source: Only 6.9% and 10.2% of units encoded value for more than half the delay in OFC and ACC, respectively, while less than 1% of neurons encoded type for that same duration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about encoding duration for reward type.

claim: 80% coverage of the delay was found in roughly 1% of the units (OFC: 0.75%, ACC: 1.59%).
source: Further, 80% coverage of the delay was found in roughly 1% of the units (OFC: 0.75%, ACC: 1.59%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the proportion of neurons with sustained encoding.

claim: The distribution of delay coverage by encoding units did not differ between OFC and ACC for the encoding of value.
source: The distribution of delay coverage by encoding units did not differ between OFC and ACC for the encoding of value, but there was a tendency for higher type encoding duration in ACC (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, value: [stat = 0.079, p=0.90] and type:[stat = 0.21, p=0.025]).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between brain regions with specific test results.

claim: There was a tendency for higher type encoding duration in ACC.
source: The distribution of delay coverage by encoding units did not differ between OFC and ACC for the encoding of value, but there was a tendency for higher type encoding duration in ACC (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, value: [stat = 0.079, p=0.90] and type:[stat = 0.21, p=0.025]).
evidence: This is a statistical finding with specific test results.

claim: OFC evidenced a somewhat stable representation from 500 ms after the reward predicting cue (around cue offset) until the response cue, but the representation remained dynamic before and after this period.
source: OFC evidenced a somewhat stable representation from 500 ms after the reward predicting cue (around cue offset) until the response cue, but the representation remained dynamic before and after this period, as the accuracy was mostly confined to the diagonal.
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of value representation based on cross-temporal decoding analysis.

claim: ACC accuracy was lower overall but showed similar patterns to OFC in cross-temporal decoding.
source: ACC accuracy was lower overall but showed similar patterns.
evidence: This is a comparison of cross-temporal decoding patterns between brain regions.

claim: The reward predicting cue triggered an increase in population trajectory speed that was followed by a period of low speed, indicative of relatively stable population activity, until the joystick instruction cue triggered another period of rapidly changing activity.
source: The reward predicting cue triggered an increase in speed that was followed by a period of low speed, indicative of relatively stable population activity, until the joystick instruction cue triggered another period of rapidly changing activity.
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of population activity based on trajectory speed analysis.

claim: Strongly dynamic bouts of activity occur with changes in task stimuli, and in the absence of such changes, delay activity becomes quite stable.
source: Thus, strongly dynamic bouts of activity occur with changes in task stimuli, and in the absence of such changes, delay activity becomes quite stable.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the population trajectory speed results.

claim: A three-dimensional subspace was obtained from the value subspace method, and data projected onto this subspace was used to decode value.
source: A three-dimensional subspace was obtained, and data projected onto this subspace was used to decode value, using CTD in the same manner as was done for the full population.
evidence: This describes the dimensionality reduction method used in the analysis.

claim: More stable value representations can be extracted from the same population data using the subspace method.
source: Repeating the CTD procedure with data projected onto the subspace demonstrates that more stable value representations can be extracted from the same population data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the subspace analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The ensembles that best optimized the CTD accuracy in both regions contained only a fraction of the units from the full population (average of five randomly generated data sets: 107 out of 798 units for OFC and 71 out of 315 units for ACC).
source: The ensembles that best optimized the CTD accuracy in both regions contained only a fraction of the units from the full population (average of five randomly generated data sets: 107 out of 798 units for OFC and 71 out of 315 units for ACC).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the ensemble selection analysis.

claim: Greater numbers of units did not improve performance, likely because many of these modified their value encoding over time and did not provide a stable signal.
source: Greater numbers of units did not improve performance, likely because many of these modified their value encoding over time and did not provide a stable signal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of why smaller ensembles performed better.

claim: The most stability with highest accuracies was obtained with a combination of the subspace and best ensemble approaches.
source: While the subspace and best ensemble approaches both found somewhat stable value representations, the most stability with highest accuracies was obtained with a combination of these methods.
evidence: This is a finding comparing different analysis methods.

claim: When CTD is applied to a neural population, the representation may appear to be partially dynamic, yet it is possible to find a subspace of the population activity that defines a completely stable representation across time.
source: This demonstrates that when CTD is applied to a neural population, the representation may appear to be partially dynamic, yet it is possible to find a subspace of the population activity that defines a completely stable representation across time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined subspace and ensemble analysis.

claim: Combining subspace and ensemble procedures is a promising method to extract extremely stable representations of task variables.
source: In addition, combining subspace and ensemble procedures is a promising method to extract extremely stable representations of task variables.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion based on the analysis results.

claim: A dynamic representation of value was obtained by selecting the neurons with the ensemble method that maximized a 'locality' score.
source: A dynamic representation of value was obtained by selecting the neurons with the ensemble method described above that maximized this measure.
evidence: This describes the method used to extract dynamic representations.

claim: The resulting CTD accuracy displays the main feature of a strongly local and dynamic representation of value, where higher accuracy is confined to the diagonal.
source: The resulting CTD accuracy displays the main feature of a strongly local and dynamic representation of value, where higher accuracy is confined to the diagonal (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C for variable type).
evidence: This describes the result of the dynamic ensemble analysis shown in the figures.

claim: A dynamic subspace encoding local value representations can be extracted from the same neural population that encodes value in a very stable way.
source: This result demonstrates that a dynamic subspace encoding local value representations can be extracted from the same neural population that encodes value in a very stable way.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the coexistence of stable and dynamic representations.

claim: The overlap in units between dynamic and stable ensembles was found to be at chance levels for all ensemble instances.
source: Indeed, the overlap in units was found to be at chance levels for all ensemble instances obtained by cross-validation and data sets in both regions (25 instances from five-fold cross-validation and five data sets; χ2 test of independence with p≤0.01 and multi-test false discovery rate correction).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the independence of stable and dynamic ensembles.

claim: Time could be predicted accurately from neural population activity, supporting the notion of a robust representation of time in the neural population activity.
source: To further demonstrate that the activity in both of these areas is dynamic and supports the encoding of time, we regressed the index of time bins from 500 ms before the reward predicting cue onset until 500 ms after reward delivery with a simple linear regression from the neural population activity (Figure 6B). Indeed, time could be predicted accurately, supporting the notion of a robust representation of time in the neural population activity.
evidence: This is a finding from a regression analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Encoding strength and encoding duration were highly correlated with subspace weights.
source: Both measures were highly correlated with subspace weights (Figure 7A, left and middle) indicating a clear link between encoding strength/duration and contributions to the value subspace.
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A stability measure that includes the duration, strength and stability of value representation was more strongly correlated with the value subspace weights than encoding strength or duration alone.
source: This measure was more strongly correlated with the value subspace weights (Figure 7A, right graph).
evidence: This is a comparison of correlation strengths shown in Figure 7A.

claim: An accuracy contribution score was correlated with encoding strength, duration and stability score in both regions.
source: This score was correlated with encoding strength, duration and stability score in both regions (Figure 7B, top row).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Contributions to the dynamic ensembles were not correlated with the stability measure.
source: Finally, contributions to the dynamic ensembles were not correlated with the stability measure (Figure 7D) as expected.
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Contributions to dynamic ensembles were neither anti-correlated with stability, indicating that the contribution to a dynamic ensemble is not explained merely by an absence of stable encoding.
source: However, these measures were neither anti-correlated which indicates that the contribution to a dynamic ensemble is not explained merely by an absence of stable encoding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lack of anti-correlation.

claim: One recent study found that OFC neurons that exhibit slow temporal integration also encode value more strongly and do so from the time of a choice until the receipt of reward.
source: One recent study found that OFC neurons that exhibit slow temporal integration also encode value more strongly and do so from the time of a choice until the receipt of reward (Cavanagh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings.

claim: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) plays a key role in working memory (WM), the temporary maintenance of information across temporal gaps.
source: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) plays a key role in working memory (WM), the temporary maintenance of information across such temporal gaps.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: The lateral PFC is particularly involved in WM relating to cognitive information.
source: While the lateral PFC is particularly involved in WM relating to cognitive information (Constantinidis and Klingberg, 2016), it is less clear how value expectations are maintained across delays.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge with citation.

claim: The content model of WM postulates that each prefrontal region maintains and manipulates the type of information that it is specialized to process.
source: The content model of WM postulates that each prefrontal region maintains and manipulates the type of information that it is specialized to process (Goldman-Rakic, 1996; Lara et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about a theoretical model with citations.

claim: OFC and ACC unit activity is known to reflect expected values associated with stimuli or actions.
source: OFC and ACC unit activity is known to reflect expected values associated with stimuli or actions (Rushworth and Behrens, 2008; Kennerley et al., 2009; Amiez et al., 2006), but little is known about the dynamics in either region that could bridge delays between outcomes and their predictive cues.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge with citations.

claim: One theory suggests that persistent and stable neuronal activity maintains WM representations across time.
source: One theory suggests that persistent and stable neuronal activity maintains WM representations across time (Wang, 2001; Riley and Constantinidis, 2015; Constantinidis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about a theoretical perspective with citations.

claim: This hypothesis stems from the observation of consistent activity patterns in the PFC of monkeys while they wait during a delay to execute an action.
source: This hypothesis stems from the observation of consistent activity patterns in the PFC of monkeys while they wait during a delay to execute an action (Funahashi et al., 1989; Fuster, 1973).
evidence: This is a statement about the empirical basis of a theory with citations.

claim: In various WM tasks, little persistent activity is found in the lateral lPFC of macaque monkeys, yet the memoranda can be decoded throughout the delay.
source: However, in various WM tasks, little persistent activity is found in the lateral lPFC of macaque monkeys (Stokes et al., 2013; Lundqvist et al., 2016; Rainer and Miller, 2002), yet the memoranda can be decoded throughout the delay (Barak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about empirical findings with citations.

claim: A second theory suggests that WM involves dynamic representations and activity-silent synaptic encoding.
source: This prompted the development of a second theory, suggesting that WM involves dynamic representations and activity-silent synaptic encoding (Stokes et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about a theoretical perspective with citations.

claim: Another perspective postulates that WM could be implemented by the sequential activation of single neurons passing on information to bridge a delay.
source: Yet another perspective postulates that WM could be implemented by the sequential activation of single neurons passing on information to bridge a delay (Rajan et al., 2016; Harvey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about a theoretical perspective with citations.

claim: Mixed dynamics support robust, time invariant value representations while also encoding the information in a temporally specific manner.
source: Instead, mixed dynamics supported robust, time invariant value representations while also encoding the information in a temporally specific manner.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study.

claim: This hybrid coding is a critical mechanism supporting flexible cognitive abilities.
source: We suggest that this hybrid coding is a critical mechanism supporting flexible cognitive abilities.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Mixed dynamical regimes, with both time and temporally insensitive information concurrently encoded in the same neural population, can provide a richer substrate to face varying task demands.
source: Here, we propose that mixed dynamical regimes, with both time and temporally insensitive information concurrently encoded in the same neural population, can provide a richer substrate to face varying task demands.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on the study findings.

claim: A stable neural representation is a robust means of holding information online and is particularly useful when information must be extracted at an unspecified time.
source: A stable neural representation is a robust means of holding such information online and is particularly useful when information must be extracted at an unspecified time.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the functional advantage of stable representations.

claim: A target population can reliably read out an unchanging representation whenever it is required.
source: This is because a target population can reliably read out an unchanging representation whenever it is required.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation for the utility of stable representations.

claim: Representing relevant information in a time-sensitive manner is critical, since most behaviors are organized in time.
source: Conversely, representing relevant information in a time-sensitive manner is also critical, since most behaviors are organized in time, whether they are internally generated or aligned to external events (Meyers, 2018; Cueva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement with citations supporting the importance of temporal coding.

claim: By representing time, subjects can anticipate the next event and prepare to either process a task relevant stimulus or produce a motor output.
source: By representing time, they can anticipate the next event and prepare to either process a task relevant stimulus or produce a motor output.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of temporal representations.

claim: It is possible that the stable and dynamic dynamics are the extremes of a continuous spectrum of dynamical regimes that can be extracted by any downstream population, depending on the computational task it performs.
source: However, these are the representations that were specifically targeted by the present analysis methods, and it is possible that these dynamics are the extremes of a continuous spectrum of dynamical regimes that can be extracted by any downstream population, depending on the computational task it performs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the nature of neural dynamics.

claim: The time constant of neurons encoding value in prefrontal region is diverse, supporting the hypothesis of a multitude of dynamical regimes.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that the time constant of neurons encoding value in prefrontal region is diverse (Cavanagh et al., 2016), supporting the hypothesis of a multitude of dynamical regimes.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings with citation, used to support a hypothesis.

claim: Mixed selectivity provides a universal mix of task variables from which the representations most relevant to the task can be extracted.
source: Similar to the idea that mixed selectivity provides a universal mix of task variables from which the representations most relevant to the task can be extracted (Rigotti et al., 2013), a multitude of dynamical regimes can provide a broad range of dynamics from which some can be selected for their relevance to the task (Bernacchia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about a theoretical concept with citation.

claim: Value signals were robust in both OFC and ACC, consistent with previous reports of strong abstract value coding in these regions.
source: While value signals were robust in both OFC and ACC, consistent with previous reports of strong abstract value coding in these regions (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Rushworth and Behrens, 2008), there were also weaker representations of the anticipated reward type.
evidence: This is a finding from the study with citations to previous work.

claim: There were weaker representations of the anticipated reward type in OFC and ACC.
source: While value signals were robust in both OFC and ACC, consistent with previous reports of strong abstract value coding in these regions (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Rushworth and Behrens, 2008), there were also weaker representations of the anticipated reward type.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Findings of weaker reward type representations are consistent with findings in human and rodent OFC reporting value signals that are specific to a particular type of outcome.
source: This is consistent with findings in human and rodent OFC reporting value signals that are specific to a particular type of outcome (Howard et al., 2015; Stalnaker et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous findings with citations.

claim: Reward type was barely encoded and decoded in ACC in one of the monkeys, suggesting that different information representation strategies were adopted by each subject.
source: Interestingly, this variable was barely encoded and decoded in ACC in one of the monkeys, suggesting that different information representation strategies were adopted by each subject.
evidence: This is an observation with an interpretation about individual differences.

claim: Neurons that encode value with linear changes in firing rate coexist with a smaller population of neurons that exhibit non-linear value encoding.
source: In addition, we provide evidence that neurons that encode value with linear changes in firing rate coexist with a smaller population of neurons that exhibit non-linear value encoding, some of which are non-monotonic, for example firing preferentially to value 3.
evidence: This is a finding about the heterogeneity of value encoding.

claim: Many internally generated continuous variables, such as time, space, and numerosity, are represented with both monotonic and non-monotonic activities in different brain regions.
source: Many internally generated continuous variables, such as time, space, and numerosity, are represented with both monotonic and non-monotonic activities in different brain regions (Nieder and Dehaene, 2009; Eichenbaum, 2014; Wittmann, 2013; Moser and Moser, 2008; Funahashi, 2013; Dehaene and Brannon, 2011) and our results demonstrate that value representations follow a similar format.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge with citations, used to contextualize the findings.

claim: Value representations follow a similar format to other continuous variables like time, space, and numerosity.
source: Many internally generated continuous variables, such as time, space, and numerosity, are represented with both monotonic and non-monotonic activities in different brain regions (Nieder and Dehaene, 2009; Eichenbaum, 2014; Wittmann, 2013; Moser and Moser, 2008; Funahashi, 2013; Dehaene and Brannon, 2011) and our results demonstrate that value representations follow a similar format.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in comparison with previous findings.

claim: Nonlinear coding may enhance population-level signals.
source: Such nonlinear coding may enhance population-level signals (as it is the case with nonlinear mixed selectivity Fusi et al., 2016), and complements the rich representations of time and outcome type that are likely critical to accurately predicting multiple facets of an upcoming reward.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional role of nonlinear coding with citation.

claim: Neural network models of persistent activity have historically been implemented as fixed point attractors when the remembered information comes from a discrete number of items.
source: Neural network models of persistent activity have historically been implemented as fixed point attractors when the remembered information comes from a discrete number of items (Amit, 1995; Compte et al., 2000) or bump/line attractors in the case of parametric WM (Machens et al., 2005; Seung, 1996).
evidence: This is a statement about computational modeling approaches with citations.

claim: Reservoir computing demonstrated that short term memory is readily obtained from generic networks in which different inputs elicit distinct trajectories thereby encoding stimuli for a short duration with highly dynamic signatures.
source: Another neural network framework, with random recurrent connections referred to as reservoir computing, subsequently demonstrated that short term memory is readily obtained from generic networks in which different inputs (stimuli) elicit distinct trajectories thereby encoding stimuli for a short duration with highly dynamic signatures (Maass et al., 2002; Jaeger, 2001).
evidence: This is a statement about computational modeling approaches with citations.
